substantiveReview.observation: Frictional electrification is explained through charged-particle transfer, commonly electrons. The electron has one negative elementary charge; the text explicitly rejects assigning one positive elementary charge to every charged particle. The combined system and no-charge-crossing boundary are stated. Post-electrification zero total is conditional on initially zero total, while each body may gain or lose electrons.

Isolation is explicitly with respect to charge across the chosen boundary. The signed algebraic total stays at its potentially nonzero initial value. Internal charge transfer, particle-number changes and energy exchange are clearly distinguished rather than treated as forbidden or equivalent conditions.

The displayed q-sum atoms and equation label (8-1) remain as frozen; the constant's language is translated. The following English defines every term as a signed particle charge and the constant as initial total charge, expressly excluding an absolute-magnitude sum. This is a substantive reading of the equation and explanation, not a rerun of the already completed native math gate.

Charge conservation is explicitly different from charged-particle-number conservation. Production, transformation and loss of original particle identity are retained with the footnote marker. Equal-and-opposite charged-particle pairs and their annihilation are examples only. The English rejects both universal pair-only processes and a requirement that each product be neutral, and applies conserved total charge to the complete charge-isolated process.

The original tenth-grade physics textbook footnote about particle creation and mutual transformations is preserved and attributed explicitly to the original textbook, rather than asserted as current-course navigation.

Experimental support and the basic-property statement remain. The original ignorance claim is tied to its historical era and explicitly distinguished from a complete account of present-day theory. The lesson declines deeper theory and closes with signed-total-charge bookkeeping.
